htmlTitle: How many square metres can you afford? — housing affordability in Europe and the United States
metaDescription: Type your net income and see how many square metres you could buy or rent in 8,489 European municipalities: 22 million listings from the ESPON HOUSE4ALL dataset behind the 2026 TU Wien study. Plus 3,141 US counties measured in years of income and rent share, because American public data does not publish floor area at all.
ogDescription: Your income, 11,630 places in Europe and the United States: how many square metres a third of it buys or rents, built from open data and honest about what does not compare.
imageAlt: Two dot maps: Europe by municipality, coloured by the square metres a third of the average income buys, from red for under 50 to green for over 150; and the United States by county, coloured on the same scale by the years of income the median home costs
title: How many square metres can you afford?
ldDescription: An interactive calculator and map of housing affordability: net income in, affordable square metres out, for 8,489 municipalities and 1,251 NUTS 3 regions in 31 European countries (ESPON HOUSE4ALL, the dataset behind Sielker and Banabak 2026, Journal of Maps); and years of income and rent share for 3,141 United States counties from the American Community Survey 2020-2024, where floor area is not published and square metres cannot be computed.
ldDatasetName: Housing affordability by European municipality and US county, 2024–2026
ldDatasetDescription: Per-municipality (LAU) sale price and rent per square metre, mean equivalised disposable income 2024, national mortgage rate and the square metres a third of the local mean income buys on a 30-year mortgage or rents, for 89,601 municipalities in 34 European countries, extracted from the public ESPON HOUSE4ALL feature service (TU Wien, InAtlas, MCRIT) on 14 September 2026; and per-county median home value, median household income, median gross rent and population from the US Census Bureau American Community Survey five-year estimates 2020-2024, with the Freddie Mac 30-year fixed rate for 2024, for 3,141 US counties. No floor area is published for US counties, so square metres are not computed there.

hero.01: Copy a link that reopens this exact setup
hero.03: A third of the average income buys fewer than 50 square metres for 44 % of Europeans. The same sentence cannot be written about the United States at all: no American public source measures the floor area of housing county by county. So the American half of this page answers in years of income and in rent — and says exactly where the square metre stops, and why.

intro.01: The question is old and the answer is usually a price index, which tells you nothing you can picture. This page answers in square metres instead: how much space does a third of an income buy here? A third of the money, thirty years of mortgage at the local rate, local prices — and the answer comes out in a unit anyone can stand inside.
intro.02: The idea is not mine. In September 2026 Franziska Sielker and Selim Banabak of TU Wien published a pair of maps in the Journal of Maps that did exactly this for every municipality in Europe, from 22 million listings gathered for the ESPON HOUSE4ALL project. Their dataset is the European layer here, reproduced to within a part in a billion. What is new is everything around it: the United States alongside it, built from the Census Bureau's American Community Survey — 3,141 counties, the whole population — and a calculator that answers for your income rather than the local average.
intro.03: The American half is missing the unit, and that turned out to be the finding. To say how many square metres an income buys you need a price per square metre, and American public statistics do not have one. The Census Bureau asks what a home is worth and what the rent is, but never how big it is; the American Housing Survey measures size only nationally and for a selection of large metropolitan areas; new-construction figures stop at four census regions. County-level floor area exists only inside private listing databases, and none of the companies that hold it grants the right to republish it. So the American map carries the two measures that public data does support — years of income, and rent as a share of income — and the square-metre modes are switched off there rather than filled with a plausible guess.
intro.04: The two layers are not one ranking, and the page will not pretend otherwise. Europe's income is measured after tax and per adult-equivalent; America's is measured before tax and per household. Europe's prices are what sellers asked for a square metre; America's are what owners think their whole home is worth. Put them in one table by local income and you would be reading the difference between two statistical offices, not between two housing markets. So the map shows one continent at a time and the rankings stay inside it. Type your own income, though, and both sides are answering the identical question — that is the comparison worth having, and it is what the job offer block below is for.
intro.05: Everything is computed in your browser from one embedded table: no request leaves the page, and it works from a downloaded file. The Where the numbers come from section says exactly what was taken from where, what was checked, and what could not be made comparable.

found.02: Everything in this section is the TU Wien study and the ESPON table behind it: 31 countries, asking prices, income after tax per adult-equivalent. The American section follows, and the two do not share a scale.
found.03: The two maps measure the same thing from two sides. For buying, the authors take a third of the average equivalised disposable income of a municipality, assume it goes to the monthly instalment of a 30-year mortgage at the country's fixed rate, and ask how many square metres the resulting loan buys at local prices, taxes and fees included. For renting they divide the same third of income by the local rent per square metre. Both answers are in square metres, so a reader can compare places without knowing a single price.
found.04: Close to 44 % of Europe's population lives where the mortgage buys fewer than 50 square metres. About 28 % live where it buys 50 to 75. Put together, more than 70 % of Europeans live in a place where a 30-year mortgage on a third of the average income buys at most 75 square metres. Fewer than 5 % live in the most affordable class.
found.05: Renting looks much the same: more than 39 % live where a third of the average income rents fewer than 50 square metres, and about 22 % where it rents 50 to 75. The least affordable rental class is very much a city phenomenon: more than 65 % of the people in it live in cities, about 26 % in towns and suburbs, about 10 % in rural areas. Rural areas stand out for another reason: for 12 % of the rural population the scraping found no formal rental offer at all.
found.06: Which country is cheapest depends on how big a flat you want. Small flats cost more per square metre everywhere, but how much more is a national trait, and it is enough to reorder the continent. Rank the 31 countries by the years of average income a flat costs outright, and moving the question from 25 m² to 150 m² lifts Norway ten places and Spain nine, while Germany and Sweden each fall seven. Germany is the seventh easiest country in which to buy 25 m² and the fourteenth in which to buy 150 m²; Spain is nineteenth and tenth. Nothing about incomes or overall price levels changed between those two sentences. Only the size did.
found.07: How far to trust that depends on where the size premium could be measured, so here it is: in {{statOwnCurve}} of the {{statCountries}} countries the curve is computed from that country's own listings in all five size bands. The other {{statOtherCurve}} are small enough that the smallest band is thin, and there the European median stands in. Every country named above is in the first group. One caution the paper is explicit about: where a band had too few listings to aggregate, the authors filled it by interpolation, so a band that carries a number is not always a band that was observed.
found.08: The geography is what you would expect and sharper than you would expect. Capital regions of nearly every country sit in the least affordable class, and they pull their neighbours with them: unaffordability spills over into the regions around Paris, Berlin and Madrid despite the higher incomes earned there, and across borders around Switzerland and Luxembourg. The coasts of France, Spain, Portugal, Greece and Croatia and the tourist valleys of the Alps are far less affordable than the countryside behind them. Scandinavia and the Baltic states come out markedly more affordable, save a few urban hotspots. The map shows this as dots rather than shaded regions; the ranking and the cards carry the regional figures.
found.09: At the country level the authors name Portugal, the Netherlands and Switzerland as rather unaffordable, and likewise Poland and Hungary. There is a caveat on Poland that matters for reading the whole map: it has an extremely high share of owners without a mortgage, so the gap between prices and incomes is not felt by the majority, who already own. It is felt by newcomers: young households, and anyone who has to move.
found.10: Renting is more affordable than buying in Germany, France, Belgium, Austria and Switzerland, but not in Portugal, Greece, Bulgaria or Ireland. The authors warn against reading the two maps as a like-for-like choice: a mortgage instalment builds equity, a rent payment does not, and the security of tenure differs. Both maps describe the market from a newcomer's point of view, at today's prices; they say nothing about what current residents pay.

found-us.02: The American layer rests on a single survey — the Census Bureau's American Community Survey, five-year estimates for 2020–2024, which gives every county a median home value, a median household income, a median gross rent and a population. That is 3,141 counties and 100 % of the population of the fifty states and the District of Columbia. It is a survey of households, not a record of transactions, and every number below inherits that.
found-us.03: Nationally the median home costs 4.1 years of the median household income, and the median rent takes 21 % of the median monthly income. What the map adds is how unevenly that is spread. 29 % of Americans live in a county where the home costs five years of income or more, 9.7 % where it costs eight or more, and 1.8 % where it costs ten or more.
found-us.04: Where it costs most. By years of income the top of the list is Teton County, Wyoming at 13.2 — Jackson Hole, where the housing is priced for buyers who do not earn the local income — then Nantucket at 11.4. Right behind them sit two of the three most densely populated counties in the country: Kings County (Brooklyn) at 11.3 and the Bronx at 10.9, and those two hold four million people between them, against twenty-three thousand in Teton. Manhattan is 10.5, San Francisco 9.9, Los Angeles 9.3. At the other end, a median home costs about one year of income in a handful of thinly populated counties in Kansas and Texas.
found-us.05: The rent share needs a warning printed next to it. Only 1.2 % of Americans live in a county where the median rent takes 30 % or more of the median income — and that sounds like good news only until you notice what it measures. It is a ratio of two medians: the middle rent divided by the middle income of all households, owners included. Ask the question household by household instead, as the same survey does, and 51 % of American renters pay 30 % or more of their income in rent. Both numbers are correct, they are answers to different questions, and this map can only draw the first one.
found-us.06: Where the square metre stops. Everything above avoids the word "area", and not by choice. The ACS asks an owner what the home is worth and a tenant what the rent is; it does not ask how big the place is, and no other federal survey asks it county by county. That single gap is why the buy, rent and difference modes are greyed out in this frame. Whether an American home is expensive per square metre is a question American public statistics cannot answer — the number exists only in the private listing databases, and the companies that hold it do not license it for republication. This page does not ask them for it. It is built only on data that anyone may reuse, and where that data ends, the page ends too.
found-us.07: Five years in one number, and an owner's opinion in another. Two properties of the source shape everything here. The five-year estimate is not a snapshot of 2024 but an average of interviews spread over 2020 to 2024, expressed in 2024 dollars — it is the only vintage that covers every county, because the one-year survey only publishes places above 65,000 people. And the value is what the owner says the home would sell for, not what anyone paid: a self-assessment, not a sale price. Neither is a defect to be corrected; both are facts to be stated before the map is read.
found-us.08: How firm each county is, is published too. Unlike the European layer, the ACS ships a confidence interval with every estimate, and every county card shows it. For the median county the interval is ±5.9 % of the value; for one county in ten it is wider than ±16 %. In 187 counties — 0.29 % of the population — it exceeds a fifth of the estimate, and the card says so in words. Those counties stay on the map, because the survey did happen there and a hole would be worse than a wide interval that announces itself.

method.03: Weekly web scraping from the beginning of March 2024 to the end of March 2025 in 31 countries: the EU-27 plus Switzerland, Norway, Iceland and Liechtenstein. Where possible the crawlers targeted aggregator sites such as Nestoria, which mirror listings from several national portals; national sites were added where coverage was thin. More than 100 million records came in; after translation, de-duplication and outlier filtering, 18,360,314 unique sale listings and 3,568,849 unique long-term rental listings remained. A listing that reappeared week after week counts once, in its last version before it went offline.
method.05: Each listing is matched to a municipality, the Eurostat LAU (local administrative unit) except in Portugal and Greece, where a coarser unit is used, and to one of five size classes: 0–30, 31–60, 61–90, 91–120 and above 120 square metres. Prices are averaged by municipality and class with a weight that penalises listings that stayed online much longer than the median, on the reasoning that an overpriced flat sits. Thin classes borrow from their neighbours; a cubic spline then smooths the five points into one price-to-size curve per municipality and tenure.
method.07: The mean equivalised disposable income per country from Eurostat's EU-SILC survey (table ilc_di03), spread across municipalities with the subnational income distribution of Mikou, Vallet and Guivarch (2024). Equivalised means the household income is divided by a weight for household size, so the figure is per adult-equivalent. The authors chose income over GDP per head deliberately: GDP piles up in capitals and financial centres and would make exactly the places that matter look richer than their residents are.
method.09: A third of the income goes to the instalment of a 30-year annuity mortgage at the national fixed rate supplied by the European Commission's DG ECFIN, the latest yearly average available, typically 2023. The price is harmonised to include real-estate transfer tax or VAT, land registry and notary fees. No down payment is assumed, on purpose: it keeps the indicator comparable across regulatory settings. Annex B of the paper repeats the map for a 20-year term.
method.11: The same third of income divided by the rent per square metre from the spline. Both indicators are in square metres at the same burden, but the authors caution against comparing them directly: the mortgage instalment builds equity, the rent does not.
method.12: United States: what the source is
method.13: The American Community Survey, five-year estimates 2020–2024, published by the U.S. Census Bureau as a federal work in the public domain. Four tables per county: B25077 median value of owner-occupied units, B19013 median household income, B25064 median gross rent, B01003 population. Dollar amounts in a multi-year file are inflation-adjusted to the final year, so everything here is in 2024 dollars. The five-year file is used because it is the only one that covers every county: the one-year survey publishes only places above 65,000 people.
method.14: United States: what the numbers mean
method.15: Median value is what the owner estimates the home would sell for — a self-assessment, not a transaction. Median gross rent is contract rent plus the utilities the tenant pays, so it is higher than a bare rent and is not the same thing as the European rent per square metre. Median household income is money income before tax for everyone living together, which is neither the European equivalised disposable income nor a per-person figure. Each of the three is stated under its own name everywhere on the page.
method.16: United States: state and country figures
method.17: Asked of the same tables, not assembled from counties. A population-weighted mean of county medians is not a median, and where the real one can simply be requested there is no reason to build a substitute. So the row for California is California's own ACS median, and the row for the United States is the national one.
method.19: The ACS does not collect floor area, and no other federal source publishes it by county: the American Housing Survey measures size only nationally and for a selection of large metropolitan areas, and the Survey of Construction only for new houses by census region. Price per square metre by county exists only in private listing databases. Redfin's Data Center carries no data licence or citation permission, and its site-wide Terms of Use forbid reproducing or redistributing the service; the same series at realtor.com are marked "Copyrighted: Citation Required" where FRED republishes them, and FRED's own terms forbid redistributing third-party proprietary content for commercial use without written permission. This page is free to read but carries a banner for its author's product, so it counts as commercial. Hence: no square metres in the American frame, and a note instead.
method.21: County centroids from Natural Earth's admin-2 layer, public domain, the same source as the country outlines. Nine of them are not there: Connecticut replaced its eight counties with nine planning regions, which the Census Bureau now uses and Natural Earth does not yet carry. Their centroids are computed here from the federal TIGER 2024 boundaries as an area-weighted polygon centroid, with interior rings subtracted — a calculation on the real border, not a borrowed point. Puerto Rico's 78 municipios are in the survey but not on this map: they come from a separate survey, the PRCS, and the Census Bureau's United States totals exclude them. The reason is written into the gap file rather than left implied.
method.23: Freddie Mac's Primary Mortgage Market Survey, the 30-year fixed rate, averaged over the 52 weeks of 2024: 6.72 %. Not the latest week and not a five-year average — the ACS states its dollars in 2024 money, and the rate has to belong to the same year as the dollars.
method.25: For five countries where average transaction prices exist at some regional level, Annex A compares listed and transacted prices and finds a very high correlation, with spreads that vary. The authors expect the spread to be smaller in hot markets, which would make urban ownership look even less affordable than the map already does.

limits.02: In Europe, listed prices are not transaction prices. The study works from asking prices, and the gap to the price actually paid is not known at municipal level. Where it is known it correlates well with the listing, but it follows patterns of its own. The American layer is neither: it is what owners think their homes are worth, which is not a listing and not a sale.
limits.03: A place is one number, and an American county is a large place. Inside a city the difference between districts can be as large as the difference between regions, and the map cannot show it. A county is coarser still: Los Angeles County holds ten million people and one median home value. The map also cannot shade regions at all — the only European region outlines published at this detail come with a licence that forbids commercial use, so this page fills whole countries and marks places as dots instead. Regional and state figures are still in the search, the cards and the ranking.
limits.04: European local income is an estimate. The survey income is disaggregated, not measured, in each municipality. In several Eastern European countries the disaggregation varies little outside the big cities, so some intermediate regions may look poorer than they are. The authors ask that absolute values be treated with caution; the patterns are more robust than the digits.
limits.05: No down payment, no loan limits. The study abstracts from both. The down-payment slider on this page is my addition: it reduces the loan and lets you see what a saved deposit is worth. Loan-to-value rules, income multiples and other formal entry barriers are still not modelled.
limits.06: Your income is not adjusted to match either definition. When you type a household income, the page takes a third of the whole thing, because that is what a household actually spends, and uses the household composition only for the line comparing your income with the local average. That comparison line is against an income per adult-equivalent in Europe and against a median household income before tax in the United States, and it is labelled accordingly — but the square metres, and in the United States the years of income, come from your money and the local price, and that is the same arithmetic everywhere.
limits.07: Timing. European listings are from 2024–2025, incomes 2024, rates mostly 2023 averages, population the 2021 census round. The American figures are five-year survey estimates covering 2020 to 2024, stated in 2024 dollars. So the American side is not a snapshot at all but an average across five years, which in a period of fast-moving prices lags a current market. That is one more reason the two layers sit on separate maps.
limits.08: The two incomes are not the same quantity. Europe's is a mean equivalised disposable income: after tax, divided by a household-size weight, so it is per adult-equivalent. America's is a median household income before tax, for everyone living together, with no equivalence scale at all. Both are what their statistical office publishes; neither can be converted into the other without modelling tax and household composition, which would be a guess dressed as a number. This page does not make that conversion. It keeps the layers apart and offers the honest alternative: put in your own income and both sides answer the same question.
limits.09: Asking prices against owners' estimates. The European layer is built from listings — what sellers asked. The American layer is built from the survey — what owners say their home is worth. Neither is what buyers paid, and the two differ from a sale price in different ways, so the two layers' prices are not compared anywhere on this page.
limits.10: And the two prices include different things. The European figure is harmonised to carry real-estate transfer tax or VAT, land registry and notary fees — in Vienna that is 6.4 % on top of the listed price. The American figure is the owner's estimate of the home alone: closing costs, transfer taxes where states levy them, and agent commission are all outside it. So the European price is loaded and the American one is bare, and no attempt is made here to load the American one, because the rates differ by state and by deal and estimating them would be a guess.
limits.11: The American home value is an opinion, not a price. The survey asks owners what they think their home would sell for. That is not a transaction price and not an asking price, and nothing on this page pretends otherwise. It is the only county-level measure of housing value the United States publishes, and it is used here under its own name.
limits.12: American rent is gross and per home, not net and per square metre. Median gross rent includes the utilities a tenant pays, and it applies to whatever the median rental unit happens to be. It cannot be divided into square metres, and comparing it with the European rent per square metre would be comparing two different things — so the American rent share is computed on the county's own median rental and labelled that way.
limits.13: The American rent share is a ratio of medians, not a count of burdened households. The map says the median rent takes 30 % or more of the median income in counties holding 1.2 % of Americans. Asked household by household, the same survey says 51 % of renters pay 30 % or more. The second is the number that describes people; the first is the only one that can be drawn on a county map, and the difference between them is the distribution the map has to flatten.
limits.14: There are no American square metres at all. Floor area is not collected by the ACS or by any other federal source at county level, so the three square-metre modes are disabled in that frame. The page would rather switch a control off than draw a map of guesses.
limits.15: Nothing outside Europe and the United States. Other countries are not on this page. Adding one would take an openly licensed price per unit of area, and an empty map with an honest label beats a filled one with an invented number.

sources.02: Every number on this page comes from a public file that anyone can download without a key, an account or a payment. Here is the whole provenance in one table; the paragraphs after it are the parts that needed a decision.

sources.13: Every estimate ships a 90 % confidence interval. Median county ±5.9 %, one in ten wider than ±16 %, 187 counties wider than ±20 % — and the card names it
sources.14: Eurostat EU-SILC mean equivalised disposable income 2024 — after tax, per adult-equivalent — disaggregated to municipalities
sources.15: ACS B19013 median household income — before tax, per household, no equivalence scale — measured for each county in its own right
sources.16: ESPON HOUSE4ALL: 3.6 M rental listings, per m² per month, without utilities
sources.17: ACS B25064 median gross rent: contract rent plus tenant-paid utilities, per home, not per area
sources.19: DG ECFIN national fixed rates, latest yearly average, mostly 2023
sources.20: Freddie Mac PMMS 30-year fixed, averaged over 2024 — the year whose dollars the ACS reports: 6.72 %
sources.23: ACS B01003, same survey and same period as everything else in this column
sources.25: Natural Earth 1:50 m country shapes for both maps; county centroids from Natural Earth 1:10 m admin-2, and from federal TIGER 2024 boundaries for the nine Connecticut planning regions Natural Earth does not yet carry. Public domain.
sources.28: 3,141 counties in the 50 states and the District of Columbia
sources.31: One five-year estimate spanning 2020–2024, in 2024 dollars — an average, not a snapshot
sources.33: 31 countries; three more appear on the map without data
sources.34: 3,141 of 3,144 counties, 100 % of the population. Three lack a median the page needs — one has no income, two have neither a home value nor a rent; Puerto Rico's 78 municipios are excluded as a separate survey
sources.36: ESPON: reuse with attribution and the required disclaimer, both on this page
sources.37: U.S. federal work, public domain. Freddie Mac: "Information from this document may be used with proper attribution"
sources.38: Read the price and income rows together and the reason the layers stay apart is visible at a glance: one column is asking prices against after-tax income per adult-equivalent, the other is owners' estimates of whole homes against before-tax income per household. Both are defensible measurements. Neither converts into the other.
sources.39: The paper's data availability statement says the data is available at reasonable request to the authors. No table is attached to the paper; the supplementary files are the two maps as vector PDFs. The numbers on this page therefore came from the next best place, and the following is exactly what happened.
sources.40: The ESPON map service. The HOUSE4ALL project publishes an interactive StoryMap on the ESPON ArcGIS portal. Its maps are drawn from three public feature services on the programme's GIS server, and one of them, HOUSE4ALL_data_at_LAU_level, carries a row per municipality with the 2024 mean equivalised income, the corrected sale price and rent per square metre, the national mortgage rate and the two affordability indicators of the paper, sa_m2 and ra_m2. On 14 September 2026 all 89,601 rows were read through the service's query interface, 2,000 at a time, with the centroid of each municipality. That table, trimmed to the fields used here, is published next to this page as house4all-lau-2024.csv (10.7 MB).
sources.41: The formula was checked, not assumed. For all 78,758 municipalities with sales data, a third of the monthly income times the annuity factor of a 30-year loan at the row's rate, divided by the corrected price, reproduces the service's sa_m2 to within one part in a billion; the rent indicator likewise. So the calculator uses the study's arithmetic, not an approximation of it, and with the defaults left alone it shows the study's own numbers. The corrected price is the duration-weighted listing price with transaction costs added: in Vienna it is 6.4 % above the raw listing price, which is about what Austrian transfer tax, registration and notary fees add up to.
sources.42: What is taken from the service, and what is not in it. The five size-class prices are in the service, but the published indicators use the overall corrected price, and so does this page. The degree of urbanisation and the coastal flag come from Eurostat's LAU 2021 correspondence table, which covers the EU-27 only; Swiss, Norwegian and Icelandic municipalities appear as "not classified" in the chart above. Overseas territories, the Canaries, the Azores and Madeira are outside the frame but inside the search.
sources.43: A third is not 33 %. The paper says a third of income, and the first version of this page read that as 33 % because the slider works in whole percent. 33 % is exactly one per cent less than a third — not a percentage point, one per cent of it — and that one per cent was enough to put every figure on the page a per cent below the study's own, while the page claimed to reproduce it exactly. The default is now exactly one third and the slider reads "a third"; move it and it becomes whole percent and stops being the study's setting, which the line under the calculator says. Checked against the service: the published affordable metres are reproduced to within 8 parts in ten billion on 78,758 municipalities for buying and 5 parts in a billion on 47,154 for renting.
sources.44: Small flats cost more per square metre. The service carries prices for five size bands as well as the overall average, and the difference is not small: across the whole sample a square metre in a flat under 30 m² costs 28 % more to buy and 38 % more to rent than the average, while one over 120 m² costs 6 % and 17 % less. The premium is a national trait more than a local one, and it varies enormously, from 13 % in Germany to 83 % in Spain. Wherever you name a size, this page now uses the band that size falls into, so the answer to "I want 25 m²" is no longer a straight-line scaling of the answer for 100 m². It changes the order of countries: at 25 m² Germany is easier than Spain, at 150 m² Spain is easier than Germany. The headline square metres to buy and to rent still use the overall price, because that is the study's own arithmetic.
sources.45: Why the map is dots and not shaded regions. The first version of this page shaded NUTS 3 regions using Eurostat's own outlines, which is what almost every European map does. Their download terms turn out to say something else: permission is granted "on condition that the data will not be used for commercial purposes", and commercial users are sent to EuroGeographics for a licence. The condition sits on a parent page, not on the pages the files are downloaded from, which is probably why so many projects redistribute those outlines as if they were free. This page carries an advertisement for my own product, so it cannot promise to be non-commercial, and the outlines were replaced with Natural Earth country shapes, which are public domain. No public-domain equivalent of NUTS 3 exists, so regional shading went with them. The region names come from Eurostat's statistical code list, which is free to reuse for any purpose. The projection is unchanged: Lambert azimuthal equal-area, the family the ESPON maps use.
sources.46: Where the page and the paper differ. The population shares computed from the service ({{statSale50}} % under 50 m² to buy, {{statRent50}} % to rent) are a few points below the paper's 44 % and 39 %. The service is the project's data release; the paper's figure 3 was drawn from the authors' working dataset, and the two may differ in population weights, in income year or in the treatment of municipalities without data. The paper's figures are quoted as the paper's; the chart shows what the public table gives.
sources.47: The American layer was rebuilt from scratch, and the reason was a licence. The first version of this page measured American counties in square metres, from Redfin's median price per square foot of homes actually sold. That source had to go. The redesigned Data Center carries no data licence and no citation permission — the download hub and the support article on downloading data say nothing about reuse — and Redfin's site-wide Terms of Use grant only a "limited, personal, non-exclusive, non-transferable" right to access and view the service, while forbidding reproduction, redistribution and derivative works. This page embeds a derived table in the file and carries a banner for its author's product. Three of those prohibitions apply. So the square-metre figures came out.
sources.48: There was no replacement, and finding that out was the work. Zillow's research download carries no usage statement at all any more, and its only price per square foot is for new construction by metropolitan area, not by county. Realtor.com's county file has exactly the right fields — but FRED, which republishes the same series, marks them "Copyrighted: Citation Required", and FRED's terms forbid redistributing third-party proprietary content for commercial use without written permission from the provider. Every remaining source with floor area by county is a private listing database. This page uses nothing that needs anyone's permission, so the American frame has no square metres — and says so rather than borrowing them.
sources.49: What replaced it is one source instead of five. The American Community Survey gives every county a median home value, a median household income, a median gross rent and a population, in one release, as a public-domain federal work. That removed the entire name-matching apparatus the old layer needed — Redfin carried no federal county codes, so counties had been joined by name, with special rules for Louisiana's parishes, Virginia's independent cities and Alaska's renamed boroughs. The ACS is keyed by FIPS code, and the join is exact.
sources.50: The Census Bureau's own API is not what is used, and that needs saying. It now requires a key, which means an account, and the bulk files at www2.census.gov answer a plain download with a Cloudflare block. The same public-domain tables come through the open API of Census Reporter, a non-profit that states plainly: "Data on Census Reporter comes from the US Census Bureau and is not copyrighted." Their server asks callers to identify themselves, so the extractor sends this page's own name and address as its user agent rather than pretending to be a browser.
sources.51: Connecticut, again, and from the other side. The state replaced its eight counties with nine planning regions, and this time it is the Census Bureau that has moved on and Natural Earth that has not: the survey publishes the nine, the map file still carries the eight. Rather than drop the state or borrow a neighbouring point, the nine centroids are computed here from the federal TIGER 2024 boundaries — an area-weighted polygon centroid with interior rings subtracted — and each was checked to fall inside the state. Alaska needed nothing this time: the survey already uses Chugach and Copper River, the units that replaced Valdez-Cordova in 2019.
sources.52: State and national rows are asked for, not assembled. A population-weighted mean of county medians is not a median, and the old layer built its state and national rows that way, from counties. The ACS publishes every level, so California's row is California's own median and the national row is the national one. The page says 4.1 years of income for the median American home because the Census Bureau's two national medians say so, not because 3,141 counties were averaged into it.
sources.53: Three counties are missing a number, and 78 municipios were left out on purpose. De Baca County in New Mexico has no published median household income; Kenedy and Loving Counties in Texas — populations in the hundreds — have neither a home value nor a rent. All three are in the gap file with their reason, and any new gap stops the build. Puerto Rico's 78 municipios are in the same download but excluded: they come from the separate Puerto Rico Community Survey, and the Census Bureau's United States totals do not include them, so admitting them would make the country row mean something different from its label.
sources.54: The size premium stops at the Atlantic. The European data measures how much more a square metre costs in a small flat, country by country, and this page uses it wherever you name a size. There is no such measurement for the United States, and there is no American price per square metre for it to act on: sizes you name apply only to the European map.
sources.55: Exchange rates for the income field are the European Central Bank's euro reference rates of 11 September 2026, fixed in the page so that a shared link means the same amount next month.

tldr.sub: How much space a third of an income buys, in 8,489 European municipalities and 3,141 US counties.
tldr.b1: A 30-year mortgage on a third of the average income buys fewer than 50 square metres for 44 % of Europeans, and at most 75 square metres for more than 70 %.
tldr.b2: Which country is cheapest depends on how big a flat you want. Moving the question from 25 m² to 150 m² lifts Norway ten places and Spain nine, while Germany and Sweden each fall seven.
tldr.b3: Capital regions of nearly every country sit in the least affordable class and pull their neighbours with them; the coasts and the tourist valleys of the Alps are far less affordable than the countryside behind them.
tldr.b4: In the United States the median home costs 4.1 years of the median household income, and 9.7 % of Americans live in a county where it is eight years or more — Brooklyn 11.3, the Bronx 10.9.
tldr.b5: The American half is missing the unit. No American public source measures the floor area of housing county by county, so the American map shows years of income and rent share instead of square metres.
tldr.b6: The two layers are not one ranking. Europe measures asking prices against income after tax per adult-equivalent; America measures owners' estimates against income before tax per household. Type your own income, and both sides answer the same question.
tldr.b7: Enter your income, term, rate and down payment, and all 11,630 places are recomputed in your browser; the job offer block works out what a move abroad has to pay.

The interpretation of ESPON material does not necessarily reflect the opinion of the ESPON Monitoring Committee. United States: U.S. Census Bureau, American Community Survey 2020–2024; Freddie Mac.
